summary: Clarify queueing vs immediate rejection semantics for short-burst webhook uploads causing 429s
description:
Issue summary:
Customer StreamlineAI is observing 429 throttles during short, high-frequency webhook fanout bursts (lots of 100-200 requests in a <2s window). They want to know whether Redwood's rate limiter queues excess requests briefly or rejects them immediately when quota is exhausted, and how that behavior differs between: streaming/chat sessions, short HTTP webhook POSTs, and long-lived SSE connections.

Impact:
- Intermittent failed webhooks causing missed events in the customer's pipeline.
- Customer reports spike correlates with daily device check-in window and causes partial data loss.

Environment details:
- Dedicated tenant on prod (us-east).
- API keys scoped per-subaccount (many short-lived keys created by their orchestrator).
- Traffic pattern: 10k events/minute concentrated in 20s windows, primarily HTTP POST to /v1/ingest/webhook.

Customer question (explicit):
1) When the per-route or per-tenant quota is hit, does Redwood queue requests for a short time (soft-queue) to wait for token refills, or does it return 429 immediately?
2) Are streaming sessions (SSE/WebSocket) handled differently (i.e., allowed to stay open and buffer) vs short POSTs?
3) What knobs can they use to avoid silent data loss during the check-in window: split-burst pools, priority classes, or dedicated burst pool for webhook path?

Steps to reproduce (customer provided):
1. Provision dedicated API key K1 on their tenant.
2. Run 150 concurrent curl POSTs in a loop across 3 hosts to /v1/ingest/webhook over 20s. Example: for i in {1..150}; do curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $K1" -d '{"ev":"ping"}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/ingest/webhook & done
3. Observe ~30-40% 429 responses in the same burst window.

Customer-supplied logs (redacted):
- Response header sample: X-RateLimit-Limit: 60000, X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0, Retry-After: 5
- Body: {"error":"rate_limit_exceeded","message":"quota exhausted for route"}

Desired outcome:
- Clear guidance on whether we can configure queueing vs reject semantics, and if not configurable, recommended architectural mitigations and exact config steps for their Dedicated tenant to maintain near-zero data loss during short check-in bursts.
steps_to_reproduce: See description above for customer repro. Customer also attached a small load-driver script that reproduces the burst pattern and will share SSH access to one of their test runners on request.
logs: See example headers in description. Customer included a compressed log (not attached to this ticket) with timestamps showing 429s starting at 2026-03-09T05:02:12Z during burst window. Body: {"error":"rate_limit_exceeded","message":"quota exhausted for route"}
investigation_notes:
Support initial triage (2026-03-10): rate-limiter rejects at the gateway level when token buckets are empty; gateway does not automatically queue long-running HTTP POSTs for refill beyond very short internal buffering.

Eng note (2026-03-10 16:12 UTC): current design uses a token-bucket + leaky-window refill. For Dedicated deployments we offer two levers that matter here: split burst pools (isolates short-lived SSE/streaming tokens from bulk ingestion) and priority classes (priority weight influences refill scheduling). There is no configurable 'server-side request queue' that holds arbitrary HTTP requests waiting for refill — excess requests are rejected with 429.

Hypothesis: customer's orchestrator creates many short-lived API keys which increases per-key small-window exhaustions and reduces effective pooling behavior; combined with HTTP/1.1 connection reuse, some edge proxies may cause duplicate counting.

Checks performed:
- Confirmed token accounting on tenant shows sudden drop to zero at 2026-03-09T05:02:12Z matching customer's timestamps.
- Verified gateway logs: immediate 429 returned (no evidence of extended internal queuing).
- Reviewed dedicated-pool config: default has single burst pool shared by webhook route and background bulk; not isolated.
comments: 2026-03-10 09:14 - Asha Patel (Support): Thanks for the repro and logs. Assigning to Eng to confirm behavior and provide config options. First response ETA within 24 hours.

2026-03-10 16:20 - Liam O'Connor (Eng): Confirmed: gateway returns 429 immediately when bucket is empty. There is a tiny internal buffer (~50ms) to finish in-flight work but we do not hold requests for minutes. For streaming protocols we keep connections open but will apply per-connection token accounting; you can hit soft-limits differently.
Suggested mitigations: 1) Create a dedicated burst pool for /v1/ingest/webhook using route isolation. 2) Add a priority class for webhook traffic so refill scheduler favors it during short windows. 3) Reduce API key churn—use fewer long-lived keys to let token windows smooth. I'll provide a config snippet.

2026-03-10 17:02 - StreamlineAI (Customer): Thanks. Can you provide exact console settings / terraform snippet for creating dedicated burst pool and priority class? Also want to understand whether Retry-After semantics are guaranteed across all endpoints.

2026-03-11 10:05 - Liam O'Connor (Eng): Provided snippet and added note: Retry-After in seconds is returned for 429 from gateway and is reliable for HTTP paths; for SSE/WebSocket we emit a control frame with equivalent cooldown info. Pushed an example terraform module to customer's shared GH repo (link provided in private).
2026-03-11 11:40 - Asha Patel (Support): Marking as triage; follow-up pending customer confirmation of config changes in their staging environment.
resolution:
Pending customer validation. Provided concrete config options: 1) Route-isolated burst pool creation, 2) Priority class for webhook with higher weight during refill, 3) Guidance to reduce API key churn and enable HTTP/2 connection pooling. Explanation given that we do not support server-side long queuing of HTTP requests when token buckets are empty; 429 is immediate aside from small in-flight buffering.

If customer validates that these config changes reduce 429s in staging within 48 hours, we will close the ticket with 'Resolved' and attach the terraform snippets used. Otherwise, escalate to Platform/RateLimiter team to evaluate a short-term soft-queue feature for dedicated tenants.
next_steps: 1) Customer to deploy provided route-isolation + priority class config in staging and run the repro. 2) Support to follow up in 48 hours for results. 3) If still failing, open INT ticket to evaluate scoped feature work (soft-queue prototype) with expected timeline.
